headline: Highest risk is medium: shared project-directory writes and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways; no direct evidence of tighter isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A writes and reads the project directory by default, and its self_isolation is none; Agent B exposes a REST API and broad network egress. That creates a plausible bridge where A’s files or outputs can be fed into B, and B may treat them as instructions or data. No direct shared-channel evidence exists, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF Agent B ingests project-directory content from Agent A without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF the orchestrator forwards A’s file output into B’s prompt or API payload, B can be steered by attacker-controlled text.
mitigations: Disable automatic handoff of A outputs into B inputs.
Add provenance tags to all A-generated files before B reads them.
Require a human review step before B consumes A-produced content.
Restrict B to read-only summaries instead of raw files.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-stripping at the bridge.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches generated source code in a shared project directory and has broad network egress; Agent B also has broad egress and API access. If either agent forwards file contents or context off-box, code or secrets in the workspace can leak. The pair lacks documented isolation, so the safer choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF the project directory contains secrets or proprietary code, A can read them from disk.
IF B receives raw workspace content or context, it can transmit that content via its API/egress path.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared project directory.
Mount a redacted workspace for A and B.
Block outbound network access except to approved endpoints.
Scan files for secrets before either agent reads them.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention at the network boundary.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can execute shell commands, install packages, read/write the filesystem, and spawn subprocesses; Agent B has broad network egress and API calls. Even though B’s write capabilities are not documented, both can mutate shared project state indirectly, so conflicts are plausible in default use. Missing explicit locking or coordination increases uncertainty and justifies medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory concurrently, file races can occur.
IF B writes artifacts back through its API integration while A edits the workspace, state conflicts can arise.
mitigations: Run only one agent at a time on a given project directory.
Use per-agent subdirectories.
Add file locks around shared artifacts.
Disable package installation unless explicitly needed.
requires-engineering: implement orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A is a code generator that writes files then offers to run them, while Agent B is an evaluation/observability agent with REST API access. If B consumes A’s outputs as authoritative without verification, A’s mistakes can propagate into downstream actions or reports. The pathway is plausible but not directly documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated code, tests, or summaries as ground truth without independent checks, errors cascade.
IF A’s generated artifacts are fed into B’s evaluation pipeline, B may amplify incorrect assumptions.
mitigations: Require B to verify A outputs against source files.
Add a second-pass human review for any action based on A output.
Separate generation and evaluation datasets.
Log and diff A outputs before B consumes them.
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source and no PHI, EU PII, or regulated data class is documented in either profile. A handles generated source code and OPENAI_API_KEY, while B lists no data classes touched. With no stated residency or certification mismatch, compliance risk is limited to generic handling gaps rather than a concrete violation.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared project directory, compliance obligations may change.
IF either agent is configured to process PHI or EU PII, residency and retention controls must be rechecked.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair’s workspace.
Document retention for generated artifacts.
Avoid storing secrets in project files.
Review vendor terms before processing sensitive data.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for regulated datasets.
